title: Learning and Memory
description: How memories form, fade and are strengthened.

questions.prompt: What is the **spacing effect**?
options: Spreading study over time improves long-term retention compared with massing it
Studying in a quiet room improves recall
Memory is better for items at the start of a list
questions.explanation: Distributed practice beats cramming for long-term retention, one of the most robust findings in learning research.

questions.prompt: Which are types of long-term memory?
questions.explanation: Episodic (events), semantic (facts) and procedural (skills) are long-term memory types. Iconic memory is a brief visual sensory store.

questions.prompt: Practicing retrieval (testing yourself) usually produces better long-term retention than simply re-reading the material.
questions.explanation: Known as the testing effect or retrieval practice effect: pulling information out of memory strengthens it more than passive review.

questions.prompt: What shape does Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve typically have?
options: Steep initial decline that gradually levels off
questions.explanation: Most forgetting happens soon after learning, then slows. Reviewing at spaced intervals flattens the curve.

questions.prompt: Proactive interference occurs when older learning makes newer, similar information harder to remember.
questions.explanation: Earlier memories can compete with retrieval of later learning.

questions.prompt: Retroactive interference occurs when new learning makes earlier, similar information harder to recall.
questions.explanation: Later material can interfere with access to previously learned information.

questions.prompt: Which generally support durable learning?
questions.explanation: Spacing, retrieval practice, and purposeful interleaving have evidence for long-term learning; fluency can mislead.

questions.prompt: Recognition can be easier than free recall because answer options provide retrieval cues.
questions.explanation: Recognition supplies cues; free recall requires generating information with less external support.

questions.prompt: The testing effect refers to:
options: Testing being useful only for grading
questions.explanation: Attempting to retrieve learned material can strengthen later access, especially with corrective feedback.

questions.prompt: Recall can improve when retrieval cues overlap with how information was learned.
questions.explanation: Encoding specificity describes the benefit of cues connected to the original learning context.

questions.prompt: A vivid, confidently held memory is necessarily accurate.
questions.explanation: Confidence and vividness do not guarantee accuracy; memory is reconstructive.

questions.prompt: Which show metacognitive calibration?
options: Use retrieval errors to adjust study plans
questions.explanation: Calibration uses observed performance to align confidence and direct further study.

questions.prompt: The serial-position effect can include an advantage for early and late list items.
questions.explanation: Primacy and recency effects produce a characteristic curve under some test conditions.

questions.prompt: Distributing the same amount of practice can improve delayed retention versus massing it.
questions.explanation: Distributed practice usually aids long-term retention; ideal spacing depends on the later test.

questions.prompt: Working memory is best characterized as:
questions.explanation: Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates information; prior knowledge can help manage its limits.

questions.prompt: Which make retrieval practice more useful?
questions.explanation: Effortful retrieval, feedback, and spaced revisiting support learning and reveal gaps.

questions.prompt: A retrieval cue can help access a stored memory without guaranteeing its accuracy.
questions.explanation: Cues support access, but retrieved information may still be incomplete or distorted.

questions.prompt: Sleep can support memory consolidation but does not replace learning and practice.
questions.explanation: Sleep contributes to consolidation; learners still need effective encoding and retrieval.

questions.prompt: Interleaving is most useful when learners need to:
questions.explanation: Mixing related examples can help learners identify which strategy applies, though blocked practice may aid early acquisition.

questions.prompt: Which claims about forgetting are reasonable?
options: It can reflect retrieval difficulty, not only lost storage
One failed recall proves permanent loss
questions.explanation: A failure to recall does not establish permanent loss; interference and missing cues can limit access.
